articles.title: HackerTube: YouTube built from videos recommended by HN
articles.summary: YouTube-style UI over 6,454 videos sourced from 39,834 HN comments since 2007.https://hackertube.org/

top_comments: It's so refreshing browsing this compared to YouTube, it feels like I don't have to constantly be on high alert at being baited into some trap. Makes you wonder what kind of internet could be possible if all these tech giants weren't just optimizing for engagement and addiction.

I've been a bit fascinated by my lack of interest in the feeds that are curated for me. They are all things I'm supposedly interested in but I just am not when I see them in that format.I realised after a while that one of the main reasons I go online is to expand my horizons. I'm actively looking for something new or interesting or surprising that I might not have encountered or thought about before. I am also looking for perspective - give me a broad picture of how the world is so I can calibrate and introspect where my own perspective differs and could be updated. I want to see the things that don't fully align with my ideas.So it turns out personalised feeds are actively curating against what I'm looking for. I'm curious if others are like me or is this just something weird about me. I think it is very much why I like Hacker News format. It's in the broad areas of my interests but it is anything but curated just for me.

You know what I like about this? It's 100% pure nerd content, no sneaky influencer videos or clickbaity news.It does need a new-to-old sort though, which is easy to add in.If you watched all of these videos, you would be the smartest, most annoying person ever. Lol

> TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 / CVSS 9.8I know it's customary for HN to edit titles to remove extraneous information, but removing "Linux" here really takes away something useful and relevant. This is a Linux vulnerability. If you're running *BSD or Mac or Windows, not affected.

Some notes I've got about this:- MPTCP is not a requirement, it is a generic use-after-free.- Exploitability over the internet is unlikely, most ISP routers drop packets with IP options fields.- At least according to Red Hat, dropping packets with IP options yourself helps, but is not a full mitigation.- Successful exploit requires multiple CPU cores to process packets, so systems with just a single core or packet processing pinned to a single core are not affected.
How are Ubuntu and RHEL not fixed? Few operating systems market themselves more as suitable for servers. What are they doing over there?

articles.title: Anthropic blocks users for anything touching training larger models
articles.summary: Anthropic blocks users for anything touching training larger models

top_comments: It's very clear to me that however much you like Claude and Anthropic models, every professional user shoudl be actively cultivating a set of alternatives and fallbacks to use and seeking to ensure the overall ecosystem is as open, standardised and portable as possible.Anthropic is highly opinionated, dogmatic and idealistic. They have made a pragmatic decision already to cut loose a whole swathe of users so they can pursue areas higher up the value chain. that was essentially the original decision they made when they went after software engineering instead of general users. The fact they are repeating this over and over by continuing to carve out sets of users and usages they don't want reinforces this as a persistent core principle rather than a single pragmatic business decision.What this means is that at a higher level, their core principle is to sacrifice users they don't "need" rather than provide a broad, accessible service. Which means in turn, you have to accept that when your usage conflicts with their interests, you are at very high risk they will cut you out. If you already depend on Anthropic in any critical path of your daily life, this will be a significant issue.

Something I've seen it do recently is refusing to extract services out of my own monolith code base because it finds copying code morally wrong.But its refusal to work pattern is getting pretty obnoxious. Another one I ran into last week was it refused to start a developer session to do browser testing for a code base it was working on because signing in was suddenly against it's programming.It listed all the conditions it needed for a sign in to be possible, agreed that my code base met all conditions, but refused to progress. I tried it in multiple fresh sessions with the same result.

This user is based in Hong Kong, where Claude is geo-blocked and not available. If you try visiting claude.ai from a Hong Kong IP address, you get an "unavailable in this region" message.They are likely accessing Claude via a VPN. Doing model training work over a VPN is a highly suspicious signal, and likely triggers Anthropic's classifiers. It's not surprising that their account got flagged.

Brutal!> ParticleDB 1.1.4 claimed to be a Postgres-compatible database ... Instead, we found a library of confusion> exhibited frequent, profound transactional anomalies in essentially every way we could measure. We routinely observed the loss of committed writes, internal consistency violations, G1a (Aborted Read), G1b (Intermediate Read), and P4 (Lost Update). In the append workload, successfully appended values would routinely disappear from later reads of a given key. Our test suite inferred every kind of cyclic anomaly including G0, G1c, G-Single, and G2-item, but many of these can be attributed to more basic issues, like write loss. These issues occurred with a single server and without faults, and affected every transaction mode, interface, and WAL mode tested

> ParticleDB’s home page advertised that ParticleDB was “formally proven” with a TLA+ proof. However, during our collaboration no TLA+ specification was available. It is unclear what properties might be proven, or whether they described ParticleDB as built.

I’ve come to learn an interesting dichotomy in software:Some software is correct by construction, in the sense that the overall design makes sense and the cases that don’t work are generally local bugs.Some software is incorrect by construction, and it tends to work by some combination of luck and by carefully working around the incorrect design in most or all code paths that could expose the incorrectness. (AI can be quite effective at finding the relevant places to insert workarounds.)ParticleDB sounds like the latter category. Plenty of large projects have portions that are in one category and portions that are in another.As an aside, for the last day or two, I’ve been contemplating that the Linux kernel’s handling of folio pinning seems to be in the incorrect-by-construction category. Good times. No, I haven’t found a hard-to-fix bug that I would credibly characterize as a security or likely accidental corruption issue [0], but this seems mostly like luck.[0] I do appear to have re-discovered a bug that some massive Anthropic dump from a couple months ago also found, and it’s getting fixed. If your application does “fixed” io_uring I/O or certain types of iommu-based or maybe RDMA on a memfd, you might plausibly encounter it on rare occasions. I didn’t bother making a reproducer.

articles.title: An Italian farmer found some unknown seeds in his attic and planted them
articles.summary: An Italian farmer found some unknown seeds in his attic and planted them

top_comments: Many farmers here in Switzerland grow urdinkel - ancient spelt. In the USA most farmers grew it also until around the 1920s but then a new wheat came out that was easier to process. Spelt has thicker hulls and wears down the mill faster so the mills switched to the new wheat and the farmers all had to switch too.Based on the name I think ur (ancient) Dinkel (spelt) is even older than regular spelt but I'm not sure. All I know is that it makes great crackers but terrible pasta and ok bread but not great.

key points about wheat Gross (the Italian farmer) discovered in 1990 his attic:+ It fared better during droughts, growing so tall that it overshadowed the weeds. It didn’t need fertilizer or herbicides.+ It's height can be a liability. Heavy winds, rains and hail can make the tall stems flip over before the grain ripens, ruining harvests.+ Working with the lab of Teofilo Vamerali, Perobelli determined that the grain was Triticum turgidum—literally “swollen wheat” in Latin. Known in English as “poulard wheat,” it had originally evolved in what today are Turkey, Egypt and other nearby Mediterranean countries. And searching agricultural references, Perobelli found that it had been grown in Italy, too, until farmers shifted toward higher-yield commercial varieties. That solved the mystery of the seed bag stashed away in the attic: It had survived because Grossi’s grandfather saved some of the heritage grains.

> It also had more arginine, an amino acid that children need to grow.My kingdom for even a tiny bit of scientific literacy amongst people who are reporting on science.Not only is this absurd ("children" need all amino acids to grow...as does anyone else), arginine isn’t even one of the essential amino acids. Your body makes it unless something is seriously wrong.

I work with another team at work that uses lots of message passing, C++ virtual methods in deeply nested class hierarchies, large DOMs and off-the-shelf C++ STL containers... on a STM32MP1, which has an in-order Cortex-A7 and a pittance of cache.On the other hand, in my team I wrote my custom C++ STL containers that allocate inline, SAX-style processing libraries and an object pool with links that use index+generations like 2000s video games... on a STM32H5 with less than a megabyte of RAM.Mechanical sympathy feels like a lost art to people I demonstrate it to... and I had to demonstrate to the first team with benchmark numbers that I would not be the bottleneck between us by orders of magnitudes.
https://people.freebsd.org/~lstewart/articles/cpumemory.pdfHas anyone rewritten this for 2026?
I feel like the solution presented is just a clustered hashmap or “locality sensitive” if you’d like it.Still not orders of magnitude better.

articles.summary: Memdoor: A team of 5 Qwen3.8-27B models beats Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard

top_comments: We desperately need to keep local models competitive with the hyper scalers. I won't want to be beholden to them and their whims forever. With anthropic now restricting game reverse engineering I think we're about to cross a Rubicon of censorship.

I'd wait for more benchmarks before making any conclusions since this benchmark has only "The first ten problems of their LiveCodeBench Hard list". And LiveCodeBench Hard is a several years old benchmark. Could be very saturated

That's pretty interesting, because with the Bonsai 2 quantisations it is quite achievable to get Qwen 27B running at 50 t/s on reasonably priced gaming machine [0]. Which in turn suggests that Fable 5 coding performance can be achieved locally with a bit of clever harnessing.Although the same harnessing should also improve Fable's performance. The important thing here is the cap for local performance looks like it could be quite high.[0] https://store.steampowered.com/hwsurvey/Steam-Hardware-Softw... suggests 16GB VRAM, 32 GB system.
